name: SHA-256 Text Hash Generator
summary: Generate a lowercase SHA-256 hexadecimal digest from UTF-8 text in a browser Web Worker using the Web Crypto API.
inputParameters: Unicode text to encode as UTF-8 before hashing
useCases: Compare the integrity of two text values
Create a reproducible digest for a small UTF-8 message
Inspect how whitespace changes a SHA-256 result
searchIntents: generate SHA256 in browser without upload

limitations: The engine hashes pasted text after UTF-8 encoding and does not currently stream files or expose raw binary input.
Text normalization is not applied, so visually similar Unicode sequences can produce different digests.
SHA-256 hashing is not encryption, authentication, password storage, or proof that downloaded content is trustworthy.
Practical input size depends on browser memory and the worker client's thirty-second timeout.

metadata.title: SHA-256 Text Hash Generator | XFree Studio
metadata.description: Generate a 64-character SHA-256 digest from UTF-8 text in a browser Web Worker, with accurate integrity and security limitations.

content.directAnswer: The SHA-256 Text Hash Generator converts browser text into UTF-8 bytes and computes a 256-bit digest with the Web Crypto API. It returns 32 digest bytes as 64 lowercase hexadecimal characters. XFree performs the calculation in a browser Web Worker in Local Mode.
content.technicalDetails: The Studio sends the input string to a same-origin worker. Inside the worker, TextEncoder converts the JavaScript string into UTF-8 bytes. crypto.subtle.digest processes those bytes with SHA-256 and returns an ArrayBuffer containing 32 bytes. Each byte is converted to a two-character lowercase hexadecimal value and concatenated, producing a fixed-length 64-character result. The same byte sequence produces the same digest, while even a one-byte change normally produces a very different value. Exact bytes matter. A trailing line feed, carriage-return difference, leading space, Unicode normalization difference, or copied invisible character changes the digest. The engine does not trim or normalize input. It hashes text, not a file's original bytes, so copying file contents through a text editor can change encoding and line endings. Processing occurs in a dedicated Web Worker, which keeps digest work away from the interface thread. The working text is not submitted to XFree servers or AI providers. Browser memory and the worker-client timeout limit unusually large values. SHA-256 provides a compact fingerprint but no source authenticity by itself. An attacker who can replace a download can also replace an untrusted hash displayed beside it. Verification requires obtaining the expected digest through a trusted channel. SHA-256 is also unsuitable for direct password storage because fast hashes enable guessing; password systems require a salted, deliberately expensive password-hashing function such as Argon2id, scrypt, or an appropriately configured PBKDF2 implementation.
content.instructions: Select SHA-256 Hash in XFree Studio and paste the exact text to hash. Preserve intended spaces and line endings. Run the engine and copy the 64-character hexadecimal result. When comparing against another system, confirm that both sides use UTF-8, SHA-256, identical newline conventions, and the same text normalization. Do not compare a pasted-text digest with a published file checksum unless you hashed the file's original bytes using a file-aware utility. A visual match is insufficient because invisible characters can differ. Compare complete digests rather than a short prefix for integrity-sensitive work. Obtain expected hashes from an authenticated release page, signed manifest, trusted repository, or another protected channel. Do not use this output as a password database value, digital signature, message authentication code, or encryption key without a protocol designed for that purpose. If the worker times out on a large payload, use a streaming command-line or file-hashing tool. Retain evidence of the algorithm, input encoding, source, and expected digest when documenting an integrity check.

edgeCases: Empty text has a valid SHA-256 digest and should not be confused with a missing calculation.
Unicode text can have canonically equivalent but byte-distinct forms because the engine performs no normalization.
Text copied from a file may not preserve the file's original byte encoding or newline convention.
A matching digest proves byte equality to the compared value, not that the source or expected digest is trustworthy.

faqs.question: Is SHA-256 encryption?
faqs.answer: No. Hashing is one-way fingerprinting and does not provide a mechanism for recovering plaintext or keeping it confidential.

faqs.question: Can I use this output to store passwords?
faqs.answer: No. Password storage requires a unique salt and a deliberately expensive password-hashing construction designed to resist guessing attacks.

faqs.question: Why does another tool show a different digest?
faqs.answer: Check input encoding, whitespace, line endings, normalization, algorithm selection, and whether the other tool hashes original file bytes rather than pasted text.

faqs.question: Is the text uploaded while hashing?
faqs.answer: No working text is sent to XFree servers or AI providers by this engine. UTF-8 encoding and SHA-256 calculation run in a browser Web Worker.
